c.tagline: Egypt's Mediterranean pearl, where the ghost of the ancient Library meets a sea-swept corniche.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are often not used; agree on the fare before getting in, or use a ride app to avoid haggling.

emergency.note: 126 reaches the tourist police (usually English-speaking); 180 is the fire brigade. 122 is regular police and 123 the ambulance line.

avoid.reason: Touts/harassment at the sites; petty crime; caution on the corniche at night

hood_desc: The central hub around Saad Zaghloul Square and the Raml Station tram terminus, packed with historic cafes (Trianon, Delices), shopping streets, and easy links to the Bibliotheca Alexandrina; the best walkable base for first-timers.
The seafront district stretching along the Corniche to the iconic Stanley Bridge, lined with beaches, cafes, and waterfront restaurants; ideal for scenic sea-view stays and evening strolls.
The leafy eastern district built around the Montazah Palace gardens and its beaches; resort-like and green, it suits families and travelers wanting calm and sea air away from the center.
An upscale seaside quarter around San Stefano and Saba Pasha, home to the San Stefano Grand Plaza mall, boutiques, and beach clubs; refined dining and shopping by the water.
The historic Ottoman- and European-era commercial quarter near the harbor and the approach to Qaitbay Citadel, full of old squares, souks, and faded grand architecture; atmospheric and central.
lodging: Helnan Palace Hotel - Montaza Royal Gardens
Four Seasons Hotel Alexandria at San Stefano

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 5:30 AM to around midnight; late-night travel relies on taxis and ride apps.
transit.note: Alexandria has no metro. Its historic tram network (one of the oldest in Africa, running since 1863) is the backbone — the yellow Ramleh line heading east from Raml Station and the blue city lines from Mansheya — alongside public buses and shared minibuses.
transit.pay: Tram and bus fares are paid in cash to a conductor on board and are very cheap (a few Egyptian pounds); there is no citywide smartcard system as of 2026. Carry small change.

bus: Alexandria public buses and shared minibuses
Go Bus / Blue Bus intercity coaches to Cairo and the Delta
train: Egyptian National Railways Alexandria–Cairo main line (Misr and Sidi Gaber stations)

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center (~1 hr, timed to flights)

tip.r: Tipping (baksheesh) is woven into daily life; ~10% at restaurants (check whether service is already added) plus small notes for hotel staff, drivers, and attendants.

food.name: Grilled Mediterranean fish
food.desc: Alexandria's core ritual: pick sea bass, bream or red mullet off a bed of ice, have it grilled or fried and served with tahina, salads and bread.

places.name: Kadoura
places.note: Long-running fish house where you choose the catch by weight before it is grilled.

places.name: Abou Ashraf
places.note: No-frills local favourite praised for very fresh fish and a big salad spread.

places.name: Zephyrion
places.area: Abu Qir, east of the city
places.note: Serving Mediterranean seafood since 1929, right on the beach at Abu Qir.

food.name: Sayadeya
food.desc: Fish baked or stewed with caramelised onions, tomato and cumin over rice cooked in the fish stock; the city's defining home-style seafood dish.

places.name: Kadoura
places.note: Classic sayadeya rice alongside the grill; ask for it with the day's catch.

places.name: Balbaa Village
places.note: Big family seafood hall popular with Alexandrians for rice-and-fish platters.

places.name: Abou Ashraf
places.note: Cheap, generous and consistently busy with locals rather than tour groups.

food.name: Kebda eskandarani
food.desc: Alexandria's street signature: beef liver flash-fried with garlic, chilli and green pepper, stuffed into a baguette-style roll with tahina.

places.name: Kebda El Fallah
places.area: Borg El Arab and city branches
places.note: Widely called the best kebda in town; famous for its bouquets of liver sandwiches.

places.name: Liver counters on Safia Zaghloul Street
places.note: Cluster of long-running liver and sausage sandwich stands open late.

places.name: Bahari sandwich stalls
places.note: Old-quarter stalls doing kebda and sogo2 sandwiches for a couple of pounds.

food.name: Ful medames and ta'ameya
food.desc: Slow-stewed fava beans with oil, lemon and cumin, plus Egypt's fava-bean falafel fried green and crisp; breakfast for the whole city.

places.name: Mohamed Ahmed
places.note: Open since 1957 and the definitive Alexandrian ful and ta'ameya house.

places.name: Gad
places.note: Reliable Egyptian chain for ful, ta'ameya and fiteer at any hour.

places.name: Attarine and Mansheya ful carts
places.note: Morning carts serving ful in baladi bread to market workers.

food.name: Halawa and Alexandrian sweets
food.desc: Sesame halawa in slabs, plus basbousa, kunafa and the French-era gateaux left behind by Alexandria's Greek and Italian pastry houses.

places.name: Delices
places.note: Patisserie and cafe from 1922, a survivor of cosmopolitan Alexandria.

places.name: Trianon
places.note: Art-deco cafe famous for cakes and coffee overlooking the Eastern Harbour.

places.name: Attarine market sweet stalls
places.note: Halawa sold by the slab beside spice and tahina sellers.

food.name: Shrimp and seafood tagine
food.desc: Red Sea and Mediterranean prawns or calamari baked in a clay pot with tomato, garlic and cumin, bubbling hot and mopped up with bread.

places.name: Balbaa Village
places.note: Popular for clay-pot shrimp tagines and mixed seafood platters.

places.name: Kadoura
places.note: Shellfish grilled or baked to order after you pick it from the ice.

places.name: Sea Gull
places.note: Large waterfront seafood restaurant, a long-standing local family choice.

food.name: Sugarcane juice (aseer asab)
food.desc: Cane pressed to order into a grassy-sweet green juice, drunk ice-cold standing at the counter; Egypt's cheapest and best street refreshment.

places.name: Farghaly Juice
places.note: Alexandria-founded juice chain known for cane, mango and mixed fruit cocktails.

places.name: Juice bars on Safia Zaghloul Street
places.note: Row of neon juice counters pressing cane and citrus late into the night.

places.name: Attarine market juice stands
places.note: Cane presses working beside the spice stalls all day.

food.name: Karkade and mint tea
food.desc: Deep-red hibiscus karkade served hot or iced, and strong black tea with fresh mint; the standard non-alcoholic pairing to a long seafood lunch.

places.name: Sofianopoulo Coffee Store
places.note: Coffee roaster trading since 1908, a fragrant Greek-era survivor.

places.name: Trianon
places.note: Historic cafe for karkade, Turkish coffee and harbour views.

places.name: Corniche ahwas (coffee houses)
places.note: Open-air cafes where locals sit over mint tea and shisha at sunset.

landmarks: Bibliotheca Alexandrina
This monumental modern library and cultural center, evoking the ancient Library of Alexandria, features a dramatic tilted disc facade covered in world scripts.
Citadel of Qaitbay
This 15th-century fortress guards the harbor on the site of the ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria, offering dramatic sea views and a storied silhouette.
Pompey's Pillar
This towering ancient Roman granite column, the largest of its kind outside Rome, rises dramatically over ruins guarded by stone sphinxes.
Catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa
This eerie multi-level underground necropolis blends Egyptian, Greek, and Roman art into a fascinating maze of tombs and mythological carvings.
Montaza Palace and Gardens
This ornate royal palace overlooking the Mediterranean sits amid lush gardens and a scenic coastline, making it a favorite spot for leisurely strolls.
Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque
This grand Mamluk-style mosque with soaring minarets and intricate domes stands as a beloved architectural landmark in the historic Anfushi district.
Alexandria National Museum
Housed in a restored Italianate palace, this museum traces the city's layered history from pharaonic through Greco-Roman to Islamic eras.
The Corniche
Alexandria's iconic Mediterranean seafront promenade stretches for miles, lined with cafes and historic buildings offering classic sunset photo opportunities.
Stanley Bridge
This elegant suspension bridge with four ornamental pylons has become one of the most photographed modern symbols of Alexandria's coastline.
Roman Amphitheatre of Kom el-Dikka
The only Roman theater ever discovered in Egypt, this well-preserved amphitheater with marble seating offers a rare glimpse into ancient Alexandrian life.

train.note: Egypt has no international passenger rail at all - the line west towards Libya is unfinished, Sudan's network is a different gauge with no through connection, and the links east to Gaza and Israel have been severed since 1948 - so every train from Alexandria is domestic. Trains start from Misr Station in the centre but nearly all also call at Sidi Gaber about 3 km east, where the crowd moving for the doors regularly makes visitors get off by mistake; stay aboard unless you actually want the eastern districts. Around 30 services a day run to Cairo Ramses, the fastest taking about 2 hr 40 min, with slower trains to Marsa Matruh and the Delta towns, and the Watania/Abela sleeper to Luxor and Aswan connects through Cairo. Foreigners pay dollar-denominated fares, bookable on the ENR portal at enr.gov.eg or at the station window - the portal needs an account and is awkward with non-Egyptian cards, so buying at the counter a day ahead is the reliable fallback.

bus.note: No scheduled international coach starts in Alexandria - the cross-border services into Egypt (JETT from Amman, SAPTCO from Saudi Arabia, and intermittent runs from Libya) all terminate in Cairo, and from Israel you cross on foot at Taba and pick up an Egyptian bus on the far side. Domestically Alexandria is well served by Go Bus (https://go-bus.com/), Blue Bus, Super Jet, West & Middle Delta and Upper Egypt Bus, all running air-conditioned coaches with hostess service. The main terminal is Moharam Bek, with extra pick-up points at Gedid station and, for Red Sea routes, at Sidi Gaber. Cairo takes roughly 3 to 4 hours, but many services start at Almaza in Heliopolis rather than the centre, which adds an hour or more - buy from the company office, never from touts outside your hotel.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Alexandria as of 2026 - the Western Harbour is now a cargo and container operation, and the Mediterranean passenger lines it once had to Greece, Turkey and Italy were withdrawn years ago. Cruise ships call but cannot be booked point to point, and freighter operators are very reluctant to carry passengers out of Egypt. Egypt's only surviving scheduled international sea link is on the Red Sea, where AB Maritime runs Nuweiba to Aqaba in Jordan, while the Aswan to Wadi Halfa ferry into Sudan is closed because of the civil war.

half.name: El Alamein
half.blurb: World War II battlefield site with Commonwealth, German, and Italian war cemeteries and a small military museum.

half.name: Rosetta (Rashid)
half.blurb: Nile Delta town where the Rosetta Stone was found, known for Ottoman-era merchant houses along the river.

half.name: Wadi el Natrun
half.blurb: Desert valley of ancient Coptic monasteries where monks have lived continuously since the 4th century.

full.name: Cairo and Giza Pyramids
full.blurb: Egypt's capital and the last surviving Wonder of the Ancient World, the Great Pyramids and Sphinx at Giza.
